metadata.title: Separating PIAAC competencies from general cognitive skills: A dimensionality and explanatory analysis

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses German PIAAC 2012 participants who completed additional computer-based assessments in 2015–2016 under the PIAAC-L longitudinal study framework. The analyses are conducted in Mplus using structural equation modeling with categorical items (MLR estimator) and auxiliary variables for adaptive testlet selection (education level, native speaker status, and computer-based core task passing score). The manuscript does not report the use of PIAAC sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme, and it does not name any weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT). Because the modeling focuses on latent-factor dimensionality and regression/correlation relations rather than population-representative estimation, the paper’s results should be interpreted as evidence for construct validity within the analyzed German subsample rather than as nationally weighted estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: PIAAC literacy and numeracy are modeled via IRT-based latent factors and structural equation models with categorical items, and the paper treats missingness as arising from the adaptive test design (testlet selection). The authors explicitly address missingness under a missing-at-random (MAR) assumption by including auxiliary variables responsible for testlet selection, and they use Mplus (MLR) to handle the resulting missingness in the measurement model. Because the study does not use PV-based achievement scores as the dependent variables, PV handling is not applicable; instead, missingness is handled through the SEM/IRT framework under MAR.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample consists of N=903 German PIAAC 2012 participants who, in the PIAAC-L longitudinal study, completed in 2015 the computer-based PIAAC literacy and numeracy tests (random assignment to competence domains) and in 2016 completed the SOEP Symbol-Digit test (perceptual speed) and the number series reasoning test. Inclusion required completion of one or both PIAAC competence assessments plus completion of the perceptual speed and reasoning tests; the paper does not report additional exclusions beyond the availability of these assessments. Missingness in non-administered adaptive testlet items is addressed by including auxiliary variables used for adaptive testlet selection (education level, native speaker status, and computer-based assessment core passing score) so that the MAR assumption is considered justifiable for not-administered items.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2012 (Germany) literacy competence + reasoning + perceptual speed (PIAAC-L subsample; assessments in 2015–2016)
main_findings.target_variable: PIAAC literacy latent factor (domain-specific nested factor)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Dimensionality: three-nested-factor model best by AIC/BIC/BIC(adj); literacy nested factor variance (σ2(SE)=2.88(1.00), p=.004). Explanatory relations (three nested-factor model): age not predictive for literacy (β=-0.08, p=.400); learning opportunities positively predictive for literacy nested factor (educational attainment β=0.33, p<.001; years in education β=0.24, p=.008; books at age 16 β=0.30, p<.001). Skill use: literacy in leisure positively correlated with literacy nested factor (r=0.241, p<.001); numeracy at work not significant for literacy nested factor (r=-0.041, p=.589).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2012 (Germany) literacy competence data together with reasoning and perceptual speed in the PIAAC-L subsample, the study leveraged age, formal/informal learning opportunities, and skill-use indicators to explain the domain-specific nested factor for PIAAC literacy, finding that age was not predictive while educational attainment, years in education, books at age 16, and more frequent literacy-related skill use were positively related to the literacy nested factor. This indicates that PIAAC literacy scores can be interpreted as reflecting learnable, knowledge-based domain-specific skills (at least in the German adult sample), supporting policy emphasis on adult learning opportunities and literacy-relevant environments rather than treating literacy as purely general cognitive ability.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2012 (Germany) numeracy competence + reasoning + perceptual speed (PIAAC-L subsample; assessments in 2015–2016)
main_findings.target_variable: PIAAC numeracy latent factor (domain-specific nested factor)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Dimensionality: three-nested-factor model best by AIC/BIC/BIC(adj); numeracy nested factor variance (σ2(SE)=5.61(3.65), p=.124) not significant; in the four-dimensional model all items loaded on specified factors. Explanatory relations (three nested-factor model): age not predictive for numeracy (β=0.08, p=.576). Learning opportunities: educational attainment not predictive for numeracy nested factor (β=0.16, p=.130); years in education β=0.07, p=.602; books at age 16 β=0.13, p=.129. Skill use: numeracy at work positively correlated with numeracy nested factor (r=0.191, p=.003) while literacy in leisure not significant for numeracy nested factor (r=0.06, p=.472).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2012 (Germany) numeracy competence data together with reasoning and perceptual speed in the PIAAC-L subsample, the study leveraged age, formal/informal learning opportunities, and skill-use indicators to explain the domain-specific nested factor for PIAAC numeracy, finding that age was not predictive but learning opportunities were not significantly related to the numeracy nested factor while numeracy skill use at work was positively related. This indicates that PIAAC numeracy scores are less clearly separable as learnable, knowledge-based domain-specific skills than literacy in this adult sample, suggesting that adult numeracy interventions and measurement interpretation may require more targeted validation and possibly stronger domain-specific learning pathways.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses a German PIAAC 2012 subsample (N=903) from the PIAAC-L longitudinal design, combining PIAAC literacy and numeracy competence tests (administered in 2015 with adaptive testlet selection) with a reasoning test (number series) and a perceptual speed test (SOEP Symbol-Digit) administered in 2016. Rather than predicting outcomes with ML, the authors fit CFA/bifactor-(S−1) dimensionality models in Mplus (MLR estimator) to separate a common factor (interpreted as close to fluid reasoning) from nested domain-specific factors for literacy, numeracy, and perceptual speed. The best-fitting three-nested-factor model supports additional shared variance for literacy beyond overlaps with reasoning and perceptual speed (literacy nested variance σ2(SE)=2.88(1.00), p=.004), while numeracy’s nested variance is not significant (σ2(SE)=5.61(3.65), p=.124). In explanatory regressions, age predicts the common factor and perceptual speed but not the literacy/numeracy nested factors; learning opportunities significantly predict literacy nested factors (e.g., educational attainment β=0.33, p<.001) but not numeracy nested factors. Limitations include cross-sectional inference for age relations and the fact that results are validated for German adults only; additionally, the paper does not use PV-based achievement modeling, and missingness is handled via SEM/IRT under MAR assumptions for adaptive testlet selection.
